headline: Aseon Labs' robotic pit stops for robotaxis raise $10M
summary: Aseon Labs raises $10M for parking space-sized pods to inspect, clean, and charge robotaxis, reducing deadhead miles.
details: Aseon Labs, a Redwood City, California-based startup, has raised $10 million in a seed round to develop parking space-sized automated pods for the robotaxi industry. These pods, called robotic pit stops, aim to reduce deadhead miles driven by robotaxis without a paying passenger.

The pods are designed to inspect, clean, and charge robotaxis, and can be scattered throughout cities. They include cameras to inspect vehicles and robotic arms to retrieve lost items and clean interiors.
The seed funds will be used to build five prototypes of these pods, grow Aseon Labs' six-person robotics and engineering team to about a dozen, and secure real estate for its network.
Aseon Labs co-founder and CEO George Kalligeros said the goal is to increase utilization of robotaxis to reach economic parity with ride-hailing services.

headline_marked: NASA's TESS finds [[2 'cotton candy' planets]] in one system
headline: NASA's TESS finds 2 'cotton candy' planets in one system
summary: The planets, TOI-791 b and c, are as large as gas giants but have extremely low density
details: NASA's TESS spacecraft has discovered two exoplanets, TOI-791 b and c, with densities comparable to cotton candy. They are as large as gas giants like Jupiter but have much lower masses.
TOI-791 b is nearly the same size as Jupiter but only has 3% of its mass, while TOI-791 c is larger than Jupiter with only 5.9% of its mass. These 'super puffy' planets are rare finds.

The discovery was made by a team led by George Dansfield of Oxford University's Department of Physics, who studied data provided by TESS. The team gathered 1,122 days of data over seven years to make the discovery.

The planets have unusually long orbits and are locked in an orbit around their star that has them tugging on each other. This affects the timing of their transits around their host star, which scientists used to calculate their masses.
Researchers are hoping to learn more about the chemical makeup of the planets' atmospheres, how their spin affects their shape, and ultimately, how 'cotton candy' planets like them form.
caption:
